What it does

Counting instead of storing the board
The cell is on the main diagonal / the anti-diagonal of a 3×3 board
A line holding three marks of one player has net ±3
No winner: full board is a draw, otherwise the game goes on

p: Opposing marks cancel, so a line reaches ±3 only when all three cells belong to one player. This avoids storing the board and checks only the lines through the last move.

1275.takeaway: Signed counters per row, column and diagonal: a value of ±3 means a win.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Packs the matrix into one integer: cell (i, j) is bit i·n + j
For each cell, the bits flipped by pressing it: itself and its in-grid neighbours
XOR (exclusive or) flips exactly the bits in the mask
BFS (Breadth-First Search) over states: the first time 0 is reached is the minimum number of flips
Shortest path in a state graph

p: `[[0,0],[0,1]]` is the integer `8` (binary `1000`); the zero matrix is 0. States reached by BFS layer (as 4-bit masks):

blocks.h: Why BFS over bitmasks works here
p: With at most 9 cells there are at most 2^9 = 512 states, and each of the cells gives one transition. BFS finds the fewest flips. Flipping a cell twice cancels, so each cell is pressed 0 or 1 times in an optimal solution; the BFS covers all those combinations implicitly.

1284.takeaway: Bitmask BFS: states are the whole board packed in an integer; each press XORs a precomputed mask.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: A value occupying more than 25% of the array covers more than n/4 positions in a row
In a sorted array, equal values at distance `step` mean the whole stretch between them is that value, so it appears at least step + 1 times
Sorted array: check a fixed gap
Keeps i + step inside the array

blocks.h: Why does the gap test find it?
p: The special value appears more than n/4 times, in one contiguous block of length at least step + 1. Inside that block some i has arr[i] and arr[i + step] both inside, so they are equal. For other values the gap test can fire only on a block of at least step + 1 elements, which would also exceed 25%, and the problem guarantees exactly one such value.

bullets: Time: O(n). A binary search per candidate gives O(log n).

1287.takeaway: In a sorted array, a value over 25% shows up as arr[i] == arr[i + n//4].

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Appends one bit on the right: shift the number left (×2) and add the new bit
Parsing a binary number digit by digit

blocks.h: Why no need to know the length?
p: The most significant bit comes first, and each step multiplies what was read so far by 2. The place value of earlier bits grows automatically, so no powers of 2 and no length are needed (Horner's rule).

1290.takeaway: Horner's rule on the list: v = 2v + bit.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: BFS (Breadth-First Search) state: position plus how many obstacle removals remain
Adding a resource count to the state
Entering an obstacle (1) costs one removal, an empty cell (0) costs nothing
nl >= 0 and (a, b, nl) not in seen
Only affordable moves, and each (cell, remaining) state at most once
k >= m + n - 2: return m + n - 2
Shortcut: with enough removals, the straight Manhattan route always works

p: 5×3 grid, k = 1. BFS layers (number of states, and the first few as (row, col, removals left)):
bullets: The goal (4, 2) is reached after 6 steps.

blocks.h: Why must `left` be part of the state?
p: Arriving at a cell with 1 removal left is better than arriving with 0, since the former can still break a wall later. Treating only the cell as visited would discard the better arrival if it came second. States with different `left` are different, so both are kept.

1293.takeaway: BFS over (row, column, removals left): entering an obstacle spends one removal.

What it does

Smallest remaining number must start a group
Not enough of y to continue c groups
Uses c cards of y at once

bullets: All counts reach 0, so the answer is True: `[1,2,3,4]` and `[3,4,5,6]`.

blocks.h: Why the smallest number must start a group
p: Nothing smaller remains, so it cannot be in the middle of a run; it must be the first number of its group. Repeating this forced choice either finishes or finds a missing number.

bullets: Time: O(n log n) for the sort over distinct values.

1296.takeaway: Greedy from the smallest value: it must start a consecutive group of k.

What it does

Reset for every level, so after the loop `total` holds the LAST level's sum
Keeping only the final layer's value

p: Tree `[1,2,3,4,5,null,6,7,null,null,null,null,8]`:
bullets: The last level is the deepest, so its sum, 15, is returned.

blocks.h: Why is no explicit 'deepest level' variable needed?
p: The loop ends when the queue is empty, which happens right after the deepest level is processed. `total` was overwritten at the start of each level, so it still holds the deepest level's sum.

1302.takeaway: Level-order BFS that resets the sum each level; the last value of total is the deepest level's sum.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: For each left end `lo`, the furthest right end of any tap starting there; this turns taps into jump lengths
Reducing intervals to a Jump Game
Furthest point reachable from any position seen so far
At the edge of the area covered by the taps opened so far, another tap is required
No tap extends the coverage: a gap that cannot be watered

p: `n = 5`, `ranges = [3,4,1,1,0,0]` (tap i covers [i − r, i + r]):

blocks.h: Why is this Jump Game II?
p: Each tap covering [lo, hi] acts as a jump from position lo to anything up to hi. Minimum taps equals minimum jumps from 0 to n, solved greedily: always extend to the furthest reachable point, and count a jump when you pass the current boundary.

1326.takeaway: Convert taps to 'furthest right end per left end', then run the greedy Jump Game II.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Minimum total difficulty to finish jobs i.. in exactly `days` days
All remaining jobs on the last day; its difficulty is their maximum
Difficulty of today's block grows as it takes jobs i..j
Leaves at least one job for each remaining day

p: `[6,5,4,3,2,1]`, `d = 2`: where to split between day 1 and day 2:

blocks.h: Why must the jobs stay in order?
p: Job j depends on all earlier jobs, so each day takes a contiguous block. The DP therefore only chooses where each block ends, rather than which jobs go where.

bullets: Time: O(n² · d): n·d states, up to n transitions each.

1335.takeaway: Partition DP: choose where each day's contiguous block ends; day cost is the block's maximum.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Hour hand base angle: 12 hours = 360°, so 30° per hour, and 12 maps to 0
The hour hand also moves 0.5° each minute (30° per 60 minutes)
A detail that is easy to forget
The angle between the hands is the smaller of the two arcs

bullets: 12:30 gives 165.0: the hour hand sits 15° past 12, the minute hand at 180°.

p: The absolute difference can exceed 180° (for example 270°), but the angle between two hands is always taken as the smaller one, which is 360° minus the difference.

1344.takeaway: Hour hand = 30·h + 0.5·m, minute hand = 6·m; answer is min(d, 360 − d).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Subtracts t's counts from s's counts in place; counts may become negative (unlike the `-` operator, which drops them)
sum(v for v in cnt.values() if v > 0)
Letters s has too many of: each needs one replacement

p: `s = "bab"`, `t = "aba"`:

head: letter
count in s − count in t

bullets: Positive total = 1: replace one `b` with `a` (the negative `a` entry is the matching shortage).

blocks.h: Why count only the positive side?
p: s and t have the same length, so the total surplus equals the total shortage. Every replacement fixes one surplus letter and one shortage at once, so the number of replacements equals the sum of positives (equivalently, the absolute sum divided by 2).

1347.takeaway: Counter difference: replacements needed = total letters s has in surplus over t.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: A min-heap (smallest item first) of the end days of events that have started and are still open
Always pick the event that expires soonest
Nothing to attend: jump to the next start day
Attend the event with the earliest end
while heap and heap[0] < day: heappop

blocks.h: Why attend the event that ends first?
p: Among open events, the one expiring soonest has the least chance later, while the others can still be attended on a later day. Choosing it first can never lose an event compared with any other choice (an exchange argument).

1353.takeaway: Sweep through days with a min-heap of end days: attend the earliest-ending open event each day.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: With one order there is exactly one valid sequence (pickup, then delivery)
Number of ways to insert order i's pickup and delivery into a valid sequence of 2(i−1) items (derivation below)

p: Number of valid sequences for the first i orders:

With 2(i−1) items already placed there are 2i − 1 gaps (before the first item, between items, and after the last). Put the pickup in gap g (g = 1..2i−1); the delivery must come after it, so it can go in any of the 2i − g gaps at or after the pickup's position. Summing over g gives (2i−1) + (2i−2) + … + 1 = (2i−1)·2i/2 = (2i−1)·i.

bullets: Space: O(1). The closed form is (2n)! / 2ⁿ.

1359.takeaway: Insert each new order into the existing sequence: (2i − 1)·i ways, multiplied over i.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: cost = dist + (0 if grid[i][j] == d + 1 else 1)
Following the arrow costs 0; changing the sign to go another way costs 1
0-1 BFS (Breadth-First Search): a zero-cost move goes to the FRONT of the double-ended queue, a cost-1 move to the back
Shortest paths when weights are only 0 or 1
Relaxation: update only if a cheaper way was found

p: Grid rows `1111 / 2222 / 1111 / 2222`. Final minimum cost to each cell:

With only costs 0 and 1, a double-ended queue keeps nodes in nondecreasing distance order: zero-cost moves are processed immediately (front), cost-1 moves wait (back). This gives Dijkstra's result in O(V + E) instead of O((V + E) log V).

1368.takeaway: 0-1 BFS with a deque: free moves go to the front, paid moves to the back.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Transposes: yields the columns as tuples
Chained comparison: v is the minimum of its row and the maximum of its column

bullets: 15 is the minimum of its row and the maximum of its column.

blocks.h: Why precompute row minimums and column maximums?
p: Checking each cell against its whole row and column would cost O(m·n·(m+n)). Computing the 2 sets of extremes first makes each cell a constant-time comparison, for O(m·n) overall.

1380.takeaway: Precompute row minimums and column maximums; a lucky number equals both.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Engineers ordered by efficiency, highest first
Fixing the minimum efficiency by sort order
Min-heap of the speeds in the team (smallest speed pops first)
If the team exceeds k, drop the slowest engineer
Team performance with e as the current (smallest so far) efficiency
Applied once at the end; `best` itself is kept exact so the maximum comparison is correct

p: `speed = [2,10,3,1,5,8]`, `efficiency = [5,4,3,9,7,2]`, k = 2. Engineers by efficiency, high to low:

A team's efficiency is its minimum. Going down the sorted order, the current engineer has the lowest efficiency so far, so every engineer already added can join without lowering it. For that fixed efficiency, the best team takes the k largest speeds among those added, hence the min-heap that discards the smallest.

1383.takeaway: Sort by efficiency descending; keep the k fastest engineers in a min-heap; evaluate sum × current efficiency.

What it does

Inserts v before position i, shifting later items right (O(n))
Placing at an index in order

blocks.h: Why does inserting in order work?
p: The index of each element refers to the array at the time of its insertion, so replaying the operations in sequence gives exactly the intended result, shifting earlier elements as needed.

bullets: Time: O(n²) in the worst case because of shifting.

1389.takeaway: Replay the inserts: list.insert shifts later elements, matching the problem's rules.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Length of the longest proper prefix of s[:i+1] that is also its suffix (the KMP (Knuth–Morris–Pratt) failure table)
Length of the current matched prefix
while k and s[i] != s[k]: k = lps[k-1]
On a mismatch, fall back to the next shorter border instead of starting over
The longest happy prefix is the longest proper border of the whole string

p: `"level"`:
bullets: `lps[-1] = 1`: the longest prefix equal to a suffix (not the whole string) is `"l"`.

blocks.h: Why is the fall-back correct and linear?
p: Any border of s[:i] that could extend with s[i] is a border of the current border, so jumping to `lps[k-1]` tries all candidates in decreasing order. `k` increases by at most 1 per character and each fall-back decreases it, so total work is O(n).

1392.takeaway: KMP failure function: lps[-1] is the length of the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix.
